query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled aging heat treatment can induce the formation of coherent Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitates that improve the alloy’s elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the same high-entropy alloy processed without the aging treatment.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single-phase solid solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents and additional elements (each between 5–35 at%) impart high configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Apply a two‐step heat treatment: first, a solution treatment to homogenize the alloy followed by an aging step (e.g., at a temperature between 700°C and 850°C for 1–4 hours) designed to promote precipitate formation.
generation.conditions: The aging treatment is conducted under conditions suitable for precipitate nucleation and growth, with subsequent mechanical evaluation performed at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900°C).
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent, nanoscale intermetallic precipitates uniformly distributed within the Ti–Ni dominated matrix.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening), thereby enhancing yield strength and reducing creep rate at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties such that yield strength is increased and creep rates are reduced relative to the unaged (or solely solution-treated) baseline.
generation.baseline: The same titanium–nickel primary high-entropy alloy processed to obtain a homogeneous single-phase solid solution without the targeted aging treatment.
generation.boundary: Applicable to Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloys (with all elements between 5–35 at%) under operating temperatures up to about 900°C; effectiveness may depend on maintaining alloy compositional stability and controlled aging parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise precipitate characteristics (size, volume fraction) and their quantitative effect on mechanical properties require further experimental calibration, and the magnitude of improvements may vary with aging parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the identical Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy composition. Subject one set to the proposed two-step heat treatment (including aging at an optimized condition such as 750°C for 3 hours) and keep the other set in the as-cast or only solution-treated state. Perform elevated-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., tensile and creep tests at ~800°C) and microstructural characterization (using TEM and XRD) to verify precipitate formation.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate under constant load
Microstructural features (precipitate size, distribution, and coherence via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., <10% increase in yield strength and no measurable reduction in creep rate) compared with the baseline, or if coherent nanoscale precipitates are not observed by TEM/XRD, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have gained considerable attention due to their innovative design and outstanding mechanical properties []. HEAs consist of 5~35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, resulting in high configurational entropy, significant lattice distortion, and reduced diffusion rates []. HEAs are typically characterized by configurational entropies exceeding 1.5R (where R is the gas constant) []. The configurational entropy equation is shown in Equation (1). where Δsmix is the constituent entropy, N is the number of elements, and xi is the entropy of each element. Due to their high entropy, HEAs tend to form single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. This unique composition and microstructure give HEAs exceptional mechanical properties. HEAs generally exhibit a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structure []. Unlike typical alloys, HEAs form a concentrated solid solution. Consequently, HEAs exhibit high strength and hardness at room temperature, along with excellent mechanical performance at both low and high temperatures [].

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as alloys that are composed of more than 4 elements with near equi-atomic percentage [,,,]. Due to their high mixing entropy, HEAs tend to form simple solid-solution phases, such as face-centered-cubic (FCC) [,], body-centered-cubic (BCC) [,,], and hexagonal-close-packed (HCP) structures [,]. With the entropic stabilization of solid-solution phases, HEAs have attracted significant attention, because of their outstanding properties at elevated temperatures, which results from severe lattice distortion and microstructural stability at high temperatures [,,]. Many refractory HEAs (RHEAs), which mainly consist of BCC-type single solid-solution phase, have been developed and investigated due to their excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures []. drafts.hypothesis: A controlled aging heat treatment that promotes the formation of coherent Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitates within a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will enhance its elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to an alloy processed without such treatment.
drafts.material_initial_state: A homogenized, as-cast high-entropy alloy with five or more elements (each present between 5–35 at%), where titanium and nickel are present as primary constituents forming a random solid solution.
drafts.intervention: Apply an aging heat treatment (for example, holding at 750°C for several hours) designed to induce the precipitation of coherent Ti–Ni intermetallic phases from the matrix.
drafts.conditions: The intervention is applicable for compositions that ensure high-entropy criteria and under subsequent mechanical testing conditions at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900°C) typical for extreme-environment applications.
drafts.structural_mediator: Coherent, nanoscale Ti–Ni intermetallic precipitates distributed uniformly within the high-entropy matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The precipitates impede dislocation motion by acting as obstacles during high-temperature deformation, thereby promoting precipitation hardening which improves both yield strength and reduces creep rates.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy is predicted to exhibit significantly improved elevated-temperature mechanical properties—specifically, a notable increase in yield strength and reduced creep rate—compared to the baseline alloy without the aging treatment.
drafts.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high entropy alloy processed via as-cast homogenization without the specific aging heat treatment to induce precipitate formation.
drafts.boundary: Valid for high-entropy alloys wherein titanium and nickel are primary constituents and additional elements fall within 5–35 at% each; effective within aging treatment temperatures of approximately 700°C to 850°C and subsequent operational test conditions from 700°C to 900°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples with an identical baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy composition. Subject one set to the aging heat treatment (e.g., 750°C for 4 hours) to promote precipitate formation while keeping the second set in the as-cast (or homogenized) state without the aging intervention. Conduct elevated-temperature mechanical tests (such as yield strength and creep tests) at around 800°C and perform TEM analysis to verify precipitate formation.
measurements: Creep rate under constant load at ~800°C
Microstructural analysis via TEM to detect precipitate presence, size, and distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (for example, less than a 10% increase in yield strength and no measurable reduction in creep rate) relative to the as-cast baseline, and if TEM analysis fails to reveal the expected coherent Ti–Ni precipitates, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of molybdenum (Mo) to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will form stable Mo-rich precipitates that impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperatures, thereby enhancing its mechanical strength (e.g., yield strength) and creep resistance relative to the same alloy without Mo.
drafts.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy composed of at least five elements where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, with each element present at 5–35 at% to satisfy the high-entropy criteria.
drafts.intervention: Introduce molybdenum at a level of about 5–10 at% in the alloy formulation (with corresponding adjustments of other elements such that the composition remains in the high-entropy regime).
drafts.conditions: Operating in the temperature range of approximately 600–800°C under conditions that promote creep and high-temperature deformation (e.g., constant-load creep testing).
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of stable Mo-rich precipitates (or intermetallic phase particles) at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: Mo additions encourage the precipitation of fine, stable particles that act as obstacles to dislocation motion and retard grain-boundary sliding. These precipitates improve the high-temperature mechanical performance by enhancing creep resistance and increasing yield strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and lower creep rates (i.e., improved creep resistance) at elevated temperatures compared to the baseline titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy lacking Mo.
drafts.baseline: The titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy without molybdenum addition.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable to alloys that maintain high-entropy configurational stability and are operated in the temperature regime of 600–800°C. The effect is expected only if the alloy processing (e.g., heat treatment) permits the formation of the targeted Mo-rich precipitates.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy: one set with 5–10 at% Mo added and one set without Mo. Subject both sets to identical processing and heat-treatment schedules. Perform elevated-temperature mechanical tests (tensile and creep tests) at 600–800°C. Complement mechanical tests with microstructural analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to confirm precipitate formation.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-containing alloy does not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., at least a 10% increase in yield strength and a corresponding decrease in creep rate) relative to the Mo-free baseline, or if the expected Mo-rich precipitates are not observed by microstructural analysis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy, introducing a controlled small addition of a refractory element (e.g., ~5 at% Mo) will promote the formation of fine, coherent precipitates during solidification and post-processing, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures relative to the baseline alloy without Mo.
drafts.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEA in which titanium and nickel are the main constituents, balanced by additional minor elements to satisfy the high-entropy alloy definition (5–35 at% each) but without targeted precipitation phases.
drafts.intervention: Add approximately 5 at% molybdenum (Mo) to the base Ti-Ni primary HEA composition.
drafts.conditions: The alloy is processed under controlled solidification and homogenization conditions (e.g., high-temperature solution treatment) and tested at elevated temperatures in the range of 800°C to 1200°C.
drafts.structural_mediator: The Mo addition is expected to stimulate the formation of nanoscale, coherent precipitates (e.g., a sigma-type or related intermetallic phase) that are uniformly distributed in the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The coherent precipitates hinder dislocation motion via a precipitation strengthening mechanism, while also contributing to the stability of the solid solution at high temperatures, thus increasing yield strength and creep resistance.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Under elevated-temperature mechanical testing, the Mo-doped HEA will exhibit a statistically significant increase in yield strength and improved creep resistance compared to the same alloy without Mo, owing to the precipitate‐induced barrier to dislocation motion.
drafts.baseline: The baseline is the titanium-nickel primary HEA with an otherwise similar multicomponent composition but without the refractory (Mo) addition and thus lacking the targeted precipitate formation.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies specifically to high-entropy alloys where titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, with overall element atomic percentages in the 5–35 at% range, and is expected to be effective under high-temperature operation in the range of 800°C to 1200°C.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys with identical processing conditions: one set of the baseline titanium-nickel primary HEA and one set with a 5 at% Mo addition. Subject both alloy sets to the same heat treatment and homogenization procedures to achieve similar microstructures except for the presence of Mo-induced precipitates.
measurements: Microstructural evaluation using TEM to confirm the presence, size, and distribution of nanometer-scale precipitates in the Mo-doped alloy versus the baseline.
High-temperature mechanical testing (e.g., elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests) in the 800°C–1200°C range to measure yield strength and creep resistance.
Statistical analysis comparing the mechanical properties of both alloy sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-doped alloy does not show the formation of coherent precipitates or if the high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance are not significantly higher than those of the baseline alloy (within experimental error), then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A controlled aging heat treatment applied to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will induce a uniform, nanoscale precipitate phase (e.g., a gamma-prime–like intermetallic) that improves elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance relative to the same alloy in its as-cast or solution-treated state.
drafts.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy where titanium and nickel serve as the primary constituents (each between approximately 20–40 at%) with at least three additional elements (each 5–35 at%) ensuring high configurational entropy.
drafts.intervention: Apply a two-step heat treatment: first, a solution treatment to homogenize the alloy, followed by an aging step (for example, aging at 800°C for 2 hours) to precipitate the nanoscale secondary phase.
drafts.conditions: Aging treatment conducted in the temperature range of about 700–900°C for 1–4 hours, with the alloy later tested for mechanical properties at elevated service temperatures (approximately 1000–1400°C).
drafts.structural_mediator: Formation of a well-distributed, coherent nanoscale precipitate phase (such as a gamma-prime or similar ordered intermetallic) within the Ti-Ni dominated matrix.
drafts.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion (i.e., precipitation strengthening), thereby increasing yield strength and improving creep resistance at high temperatures by impeding thermally activated slip processes.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The aged alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and enhanced creep resistance compared to the baseline as-cast or solution-treated state without aging.
drafts.baseline: The unaged, homogenous single-phase high-entropy alloy wherein titanium and nickel are primary constituents but no targeted precipitate has been induced.
drafts.boundary: Applicable to Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloys with constituent concentrations meeting the 5–35 at% rule; the improvement is expected at service temperatures up to approximately 1400°C, with the alloy composition and aging parameters remaining within the specified ranges.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy composition. Subject one set to the proposed solution treatment plus aging (e.g., aging at 800°C for 2 hours) and keep the other set in the as-cast or solution-treated state. Test both sets under identical elevated-temperature conditions (e.g., at 1200°C) for yield strength and creep resistance. Acquire detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM and XRD) to assess precipitate formation and distribution.
measurements: Creep rate under a constant load (strain/time)
Microstructural features (precipitate size, distribution, and coherence via TEM/XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aging-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10% increase in yield strength and reduced creep rates) compared with the baseline, or if no coherent nanoscale precipitates are found in the aged samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
